dossier.public_summary: The 1.992-hour dip repeats exactly at the star's 0.985-day spin period, which shows spot signals ten times deeper than the dip itself. The dip depth more than doubles from sector to sector and the light curve outside the dip swings almost as much as the dip, as expected for a spotted/active star or a tight stellar companion. The star also has an extremely high RUWE suggesting binarity, so a planet is not the best explanation.

reasons.why: Dip period is exactly the stellar rotation period (and a multiple = 1), with huge spot amplitudes 12164 to 12976 ppm. Period aliases and flat-bottom shape alone cannot make a rotating spotted M dwarf with this short rotation a planet because the phase-curve swing is almost as large as the dip.
Large out-of-eclipse modulation at this period and an enormous phase-curve chi2 point to spots and/or a close binary, not a planetary transit on a planet-sized orbit.

Depth varies by more than a factor of two within the first cycle alone, unlike an achromatic planet. sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source (SPOC 2-min p_constant 2.9171799553884132e-08) shows real spot/detrending changes, not a calibration offset.
Extreme Gaia astrometric excess indicates the star is astrometrically a binary or has corrupted astrometry, consistent with the phase-curve and variability.

Transit-fit density mismatch and the secondary check (best_brightening_snr 54, secondary snr -8.946) together with V-shaped bootstrap false-positives place an eclipsing binary / stellar companion as the best explanation over a planet.
